In short, local governments have strong powers of intervention over almost every factor of production that matters to businesses. Land belongs directly to the government. Capital comes mostly from a financial system dominated by state-owned banks, and from other government-controlled channels such as state-owned investment and financing platforms. As for labor, the government controls household registration (hukou) and the supply of basic services such as education and health care, and since it also controls the supply of land, it directly shapes how housing is allocated. A considerable share of the research and technology that goes into production also comes from public universities and research institutes. On top of all this, local governments wield fiscal and tax policy, industrial policy, import and export policy and other tools, any of which can have a major impact on businesses.

This “mixed economy” is not the simple division of labor between government and market described in mainstream economics textbooks, in which the government provides public goods and the market allocates everything else. Nor is it simply a case of “the government builds the stage and businesses put on the show.” It is a model in which the government and its many affiliated bodies (state-owned enterprises, public institutions, the big banks and so on) are deeply involved in most stages of production and distribution. In China, trying to understand the economy without the government is impossible.
